newsitem.title: UK: Tin seen drifting lower on weak fundamentals.
newsitem.headline: Tin seen drifting lower on weak fundamentals.

text.p: Tin is under pressure from rising supplies and lacklustre demand and is expected to drift lower in the short term, analysts said.
The bounce back to over $5,400 per tonne has been seen as a temporary blip after tin found new 2 1/3-year lows of $5,360 on the LME on July 22.
Tin edged above $5,400 in pre-market activity on Wednesday from the previous afternoon kerb close of $5,370.
"The bounce was not convincing. The market will meet further resistance," said Robin Bhar of Brandeis.

At $5,100-5,150 per tonne consumer and trade buying is expected, although volumes are not seen large enough to start a rally, Bhar said. "It is difficult to see how the market can turn around," he added.
Bhar added that the market would probably not fall below $5,000, a level at which many mines would be unviable and production would start to be cut.
Short covering and possible fund buying may be a factor as tin drifts to $5,200-5,300 and below.

"The market is setting itself up for some fund buying interest," said William Adams of Rudolf Wolff, although others were sceptical that funds would be interested, since they had shown so little interest in the past.
The general drift down in price has not been helped by the devaluation in South East Asian currencies, which have made it more attractive for the region to export tin, Adams said.
On the upside, any rise in price is likely to be capped by producer selling and the Chinese, who are expected to be aggressive sellers at $6,000 per tonne, analysts said.

An increase in production from Peru and Indonesia, coupled with stockpile sales from Russia, has kept prices at the lower end of the range. Russia is understood to have sold 8,000 tonnes of tin from its stockpiles.
Consumers remain content to buy hand-to-mouth, analysts said, adding that demand had been increasing by just one percent per year recently.
LME stocks, although down sharply from levels above 30,000 tonnes seen in 1995, are a bearish factor if anything, and analysts are predicting a rise in inventories.

At current levels of around 8-8 1/2 weeks' consumption -- or 11,640 tonnes -- stocks are still well clear of critical low levels of 5 1/2-6 weeks' consumption, according to Karen Norton of Billiton Research.

However, producers remain bullish as demand is seen rising sharply, according to studies by tin producer body ITRI Ltd, formerly the International Tin Research Institute, which sees prices rising to $7,500 by 2000.
"We remain astonished at the current low price levels," said Rod Bedder, managing director of ITRI.
ITRI is forecasting significant rises in tin consumption to 2000 as the decrease in traditional uses of tin is overtaken by the increase in new applications.

According to Bedder, the crossover point for this will be mid-1998 at the latest as tin replaces lead in solder, stabilisers for plastics used in the motor industry, acid accumulator batteries and shotgun cartridges. All of these innovations have passed the development stage and are now being commercialised, he said.
ITRI is forecasting one percent growth in tin consumption this year, rising to four percent and 3.5 percent in 1998 and 1999 respectively.
Marginal producers in Bolivia and Brazil are expected to cap any rise above $7,500 over the next five years, Bedder added.
